A.explanation: Gives about $6 \text{ s}$, far too short because it underestimates the $mgh$ work needed for $1500 \text{ kg}$ lifted $20 \text{ m}$.

B.explanation: Matches $t = mgh/P \approx 15 \text{ s}$ for the $20 \text{ kW}$ output power raising $1500 \text{ kg}$ through $20 \text{ m}$.

C.explanation: Gives $30 \text{ s}$, about twice the correct time, as if only $10 \text{ kW}$ were used or the work were doubled.

D.explanation: Gives $60 \text{ s}$, about four times too long, as if power or $g$ were mishandled in $t = mgh/P$.

hints: Notice the motor output power is $20 \text{ kW} = 20000 \text{ W}$ and the $1500 \text{ kg}$ lift moves $20 \text{ m}$ upward at constant speed.
Connect constant-speed lifting to work against weight: $W = mgh$, and to power by $P = W/t$.
Rearrange to $t = mgh/t$ with $P$ in the denominator, then substitute $m = 1500 \text{ kg}$, $h = 20 \text{ m}$ and $P = 20000 \text{ W}$ to compare with the $6 \text{ s}$ to $60 \text{ s}$ options.
walkthrough: Identify the useful data: output power $P = 20 \text{ kW} = 20000 \text{ W}$, mass $m = 1500 \text{ kg}$, vertical height $h = 20 \text{ m}$, constant speed so no gain in kinetic energy.
State the physics: motor work $W$ increases gravitational potential energy, $W = mgh$, and power is rate of doing work, $P = W/t$.
Combine to $t = W/P = mgh/P$ using $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Calculate $t \approx 14.7 \text{ s}$, with units of $\text{J}/\text{W} = \text{s}$, so about $15 \text{ s}$ to sensible precision. This is option B.
